nameStory: The name 'tree-of-heaven' comes from its incredible ability to grow almost anywhere and reach impressive heights quickly, as if reaching toward the heavens. Some say the name reflects how this tree seems to appear magically in the most unlikely places - sprouting from sidewalk cracks, vacant lots, and disturbed soil where other trees struggle to survive.
description: Tree-of-heaven is a fast-growing deciduous tree that can rocket up to 50 feet tall in just 25 years. It has large, tropical-looking compound leaves that can stretch over 3 feet long, giving it an almost palm-like appearance despite being adapted to temperate climates. This invasive species from China is unfortunately very common in New England, forming dense colonies along roadsides, in vacant lots, and anywhere the soil has been disturbed. Young trees have smooth gray bark, while older specimens develop rougher, diamond-patterned bark.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Massive compound leaves up to 3 feet long with 10-25 leaflets arranged along a central stem. Each smooth-edged leaflet has 1-3 small teeth near its base with tiny glands that smell awful when crushed - like rancid peanut butter mixed with cat urine.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies of straight-trunked trees with sparse branching, creating a distinctive 'telephone pole with a feather duster top' silhouette. Often see multiple stems sprouting from the same root system.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth and gray on young trees, developing distinctive diamond-shaped furrows and ridges as it ages. The bark has a slightly papery texture and peels in thin strips.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Clusters of papery, twisted wing-shaped seeds called samaras that hang in large bunches, turning from green to tan to reddish-brown. They persist through winter and rattle in the wind.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small greenish-white flowers appear in large, showy clusters at branch tips in early summer. Male flowers have a particularly strong, unpleasant smell that attracts flies.

habitat: Tree-of-heaven thrives in disturbed soils and urban environments throughout New England, especially along roadsides, railroad tracks, vacant lots, and construction sites. It prefers sunny locations and well-drained soil but tolerates almost any condition including pollution, drought, and poor soil. You'll often find it growing through cracks in pavement or emerging from the tiniest soil pockets in the most unlikely places.

seasonality.spring: Large compound leaves emerge late in spring, unfurling to reveal their tropical appearance. New growth has a reddish tint and the characteristic foul smell is strongest when leaves are young and tender.
seasonality.summer: Clusters of small greenish flowers appear in early summer, followed by the development of papery seed clusters. The massive leaves create dense shade and reach their full impressive size.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow briefly before dropping, often all at once. The abundant clusters of tan to reddish samara fruits become very conspicuous and persist on bare branches.
seasonality.winter: Smooth gray bark and sparse branching pattern are visible, along with persistent clusters of papery seeds that rattle in winter winds. Multiple straight trunks from root sprouts are especially obvious.

funFact: A single female tree-of-heaven can produce over 300,000 winged seeds in one year, and if you cut the tree down, the stump can send up dozens of new shoots that grow up to 10 feet in a single season - making it nearly impossible to get rid of once established!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with native sumacs, black walnut, or butternut due to the large compound leaves. However, tree-of-heaven leaflets are smooth-edged (except for those distinctive glandular teeth at the base), while sumacs have serrated leaflets all along the edges, and walnuts have many more leaflets per leaf. Remember: 'Smooth leaves that stink' points to tree-of-heaven.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its heavenly name, this tree is considered one of the worst invasive species in North America and is actually nicknamed 'tree-of-hell' by many land managers. It's become even more problematic recently because it's the preferred host plant for the destructive spotted lanternfly, another invasive species spreading through New England.
compareHints: Tree-of-heaven is the only member of its genus found in temperate North America - most other Ailanthus species are tropical. Within the quassia family, it's unique in New England for its large size and compound leaves. The closest comparison would be members of the cashew family like sumacs, but tree-of-heaven grows much taller, has smoother leaflet margins, and lacks the fuzzy red fruit clusters that sumacs produce.
